title: At Some Point, You Have to Stop Repeating the Bad News
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses how leaders should handle the aftermath of a crisis once the initial explanations and remedies have been fully delivered. The author acknowledges that people affected by a misstep need time to vent and revisit the events, and that patient leaders allow for that healing process. But it draws a firm line: once the response has been thoroughly explained and implemented, continuing to relitigate the crisis only keeps it alive and prevents real closure. The piece urges leaders to trust their own judgment about when to stop discussing the past and insist on moving forward, even against pressure to keep re-explaining themselves.
points: Good leaders are patient early on, letting affected people vent and revisit a crisis as part of healing.
There comes a point where continuing to discuss a crisis only keeps it alive.
Leaders who keep re-explaining past mistakes reopen wounds rather than allowing closure.
Trying to appear endlessly open and cooperative can work against an organization's best interests.
Deciding when to stop discussing the past is essential for a team to truly move forward.
quotes: When things go horribly wrong, leaders face the difficult challenge of repairing a reputation and credibility that is now suspect.
Good leaders are patient in this process. They accept that people who were affected need to vent, be heard, and offer their views.
In every crisis or reputationally altering event, there comes a point where the bad news is keeping the bad news alive.
Even temporarily revisiting the crisis reopens the wounds and prevents real closure from happening.
Keeping the bad news permanently on the agenda is a losing strategy.
At a certain point in time in every crisis, the bad news is when leaders allow the bad news to stay alive.
